pointers.sentence: `sync_to_async` makes a function awaitable by running it in a thread, and `async_to_sync` makes a coroutine function callable by running it on an event loop and waiting for it (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:sync_to_async`, `asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:async_to_sync`).

`sync_to_async` makes a function awaitable by running it in a thread, and `async_to_sync` makes a coroutine function callable by running it on an event loop and waiting for it (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:sync_to_async`, `asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:async_to_sync`).

`BaseHandler.adapt_method_mode` fits a method to the mode wanted: a coroutine function wanted synchronous is wrapped in `async_to_sync`, a function wanted asynchronous in `sync_to_async` with `thread_sensitive=True`, which keeps it on the request's one thread ([One thread per request](#one-thread-per-request)), and a method already in that mode is returned unchanged (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.adapt_method_mode`).
For a function, the decorators `sync_only_middleware`, `async_only_middleware` and `sync_and_async_middleware` set the pair (`django/utils/decorators.py:sync_and_async_middleware`).

In async mode `MiddlewareMixin.__call__` hands over to `MiddlewareMixin.__acall__`, which awaits the inner layer and runs `process_request` and `process_response` each through `sync_to_async` (`django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__init__`, `django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__acall__`).

In async mode `MiddlewareMixin.__call__` hands over to `MiddlewareMixin.__acall__`, which awaits the inner layer and runs `process_request` and `process_response` each through `sync_to_async` (`django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__init__`, `django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__acall__`).
So under ASGI they now run synchronously, where they used to run in the mixin's async mode (`django/middleware/common.py:CommonMiddleware.async_capable`).

If the two modes differ, the chain so far is adapted before the middleware is given it, and when the loop ends the outermost layer is adapted to the handler's mode (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.load_middleware`).

Every ASGI request that is answered makes the first and last, whatever its middleware: Django's own receivers of `request_started` are synchronous, and so is closing the response (`django/dispatch/dispatcher.py:Signal.asend`, `django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.handle`).

Every ASGI request that is answered makes the first and last, whatever its middleware: Django's own receivers of `request_started` are synchronous, and so is closing the response (`django/dispatch/dispatcher.py:Signal.asend`, `django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.handle`).

The thread can run the view while it waits inside the middleware: until the centre returns, `async_to_sync` keeps it in a `CurrentThreadExecutor`, which runs on it any thread-sensitive code the centre calls through `sync_to_async` (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:AsyncToSync.__call__`, `asgiref:asgiref/current_thread_executor.py:CurrentThreadExecutor.run_until_future`).

The thread can run the view while it waits inside the middleware: until the centre returns, `async_to_sync` keeps it in a `CurrentThreadExecutor`, which runs on it any thread-sensitive code the centre calls through `sync_to_async` (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:AsyncToSync.__call__`, `asgiref:asgiref/current_thread_executor.py:CurrentThreadExecutor.run_until_future`).

Under synchronous middleware it is inside their call, waiting in `async_to_sync` for the centre; in async mode it is idle in its executor from the last `process_request` to the first `process_response`, and the second pays in switching (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:SyncToAsync.__call__`).

Its release notes allow that for high in-process concurrency over I/O that is not the ORM's, "where no thread is otherwise held", the switching may be preferable to "pinning a thread per request" (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).
The documentation says that with synchronous middleware around an async view Django will "hold the sync thread open for middleware exception propagation" (`docs/topics/async.txt`).

A `process_view` or a `process_template_response` is adapted to the handler's mode as it is filed ([Building the middleware chain](chain.md#the-three-lists-of-hooks)), so under ASGI a synchronous `process_view` is a crossing of its own on each call, whatever mode its middleware runs in (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.load_middleware`).

The centre runs it through `async_to_sync`, on an event loop in a thread of its own, while the handler's thread waits (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`, `asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:AsyncToSync.__call__`).

The centre runs it through `async_to_sync`, on an event loop in a thread of its own, while the handler's thread waits (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`, `asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:AsyncToSync.__call__`).

It can still await several things at once, but it occupies two threads where a synchronous view would occupy one; as the documentation says, "you will not get the benefits of an async stack" (`docs/topics/async.txt`).

Together these mean that everything those crossings run for one request runs on one thread for the length of the request, and that two requests do not share a thread (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.__call__`).

The thread is made at a request's first thread-sensitive crossing, the one for `request_started`, and lasts until the request ends: every request that gets that far has a thread of its own, whatever its middleware and its view (`asgiref:asgiref/sync.py:SyncToAsync.__call__`).

The single thread matters because a database connection belongs to the thread that opened it (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.thread_critical`): a middleware's `process_request` and the view it precedes see the same connection, and the same transaction, only on the same thread.
